title: Harvard offers ‘anti-racist’ resources for parents as students head back to school
text:

DiJonai Carrington and Emmanuel Acho can throw out "white privilege" all they want. Dan Dakich claims it's an oversaturated insult that no longer means anything

A Harvard University webpage that provides resources for parents of students at the school features "anti-racism resources," including a list of books written by controversial authors who have espoused anti-White rhetoric and have suggested discrimination is OK as long as it's against White people.

One of the books is Ibram X. Kendi's "How To Be An Anti-Racist", another is the infamous "White Fragility" by Robin DiAngelo.

Kendi, born Ibram Henry Rogers, is known for racially inflammatory comments targeting White people.

Dunster House along the Charles River on the Harvard University campus in Cambridge, Massachusetts, US, on Tuesday, May 27, 2025. (Sophie Park/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

DAVID MARCUS: TRANSPORTATION SECRETARY DUFFY IS RIGHT; HARVARD JUST AIN’T WHAT IT USED TO BE

"Europeans are simply a different breed of human," he wrote in a column in his college newspaper in 2003. "They are socialized to be aggressive people. They are taught to live by the credo, 'survival of the fittest.' They are raised to be racist."

In his 2019 book, Kendi explained that discrimination is fine, as long as it promotes equity. On the contrary, he said, discrimination is wrong if it promotes inequity.

DISCRIMINATORY 'SHADOW' REVIEW PROCESS LOCKS WHITE, ASIAN STUDENTS OUT OF CALIFORNIA MED SCHOOL, DOJ ALLEGES

"The only remedy to racist discrimination is antiracist discrimination," the book says. "The only remedy to past discrimination is present discrimination. The only remedy to present discrimination is future discrimination."

Kendi also slammed "whiteness" at a film screening in November 2023.

Dr. Ibram X. Kendi speaks onstage during Netflix's "Stamped From The Beginning" world premiere at the Toronto International Film Festival at TIFF Bell Lightbox in Toronto, Ontario, on Sept. 9, 2023. (Tommaso Boddi/Getty Images for Netflix)

"I don't think White people worldwide have really reckoned with how much their own personal identity is shaped by constructions of whiteness, and how much that construction of whiteness prevents White people from connecting to humanity," he said at the event.

Similarly, the resource page on Harvard's site includes "White Fragility: Why It’s So Hard for White People to Talk About Racism."

GEORGIA DISTRICT QUIETLY TRAINED TEACHERS TO BLAME 'WHITENESS,' 'DECOLONIZE' UNDER FEDERAL CRACKDOWN: REPORT

"White people are socialized to feel that they are inherently superior because they are white," DiAngelo wrote in the 2018 book.

"Racism is a White problem. It was created by White people," the book says. "It is wielded by White people, it benefits White people."

Author Robin DiAngelo appears during an interview on The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon on June 17, 2020. (NBCU Photo Bank via Getty Images)

She also wrote that White people are always racist.

"The question is not 'Did racism take place?' but rather, 'How did racism manifest in this situation?'" she wrote in the book.

Other books recommended to parents include "Me and White Supremacy," by Layla Saad, "Raising White Kids," by Jennifer Harvey and "The New Jim Crow: Mass Incarceration in the Age of Colorblindness," by Michelle Alexander.

A spokesperson for Harvard told Fox News Digital, "The site was created by staff more than five years ago and was not developed as an official Faculty of Arts and Sciences resource."

The online page is title "Anti-Racism Resources" and the list of books is included under the "Information for Parents" tab of the Harvard website.

EXCLUSIVE: SPLC'S 'FAR-LEFT' 'ANTI-RACISM' CURRICULUM FOUND IN CLASSROOMS AS EARLY AS KINDERGARTEN: WATCHDOG

The webpage also lists resources for teaching children as young as infants "anti-racism," including Kendi's "Anti-Racist Baby," which "introduces the youngest readers and the grown-ups in their lives to the concept and power of antiracism," according to Goodreads.

"Providing the language necessary to begin critical conversations at the earliest age, 'Antiracist Baby' is the perfect gift for readers of all ages dedicated to forming a just society" the description continues.

Gregory Davis, former resident dean of the Dunster House at Harvard University, speaks at an Oct. 14, 2028 DefendDiversity rally. (L) Dunster House along the Charles River on the Harvard University campus in Cambridge, Massachusetts, US, on Tuesday, May 27, 2025. (Suuba Demby/Harvard University; Sophie Park/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Harvard has faced issues of anti-White racism among its staff.

Gregory Davis, the former Dunster House Allston Burr resident dean at Harvard, was fired earlier this year after a series of anti-White, anti–police social media posts were unearthed. Other posts from Davis supported rioting and looting as legitimate forms of protest.

The posts in question were made between 2019 and 2024, mostly on X but also on Instagram. Davis became the dean of the dormitory in 2024.

"It’s almost like whiteness is a self-destructive ideology that annihilates everyone around it. By design," he said on X in 2019.

During 2020, when tensions between police and left-wing rioters reached a fever pitch after George Floyd was killed, Davis slammed police.

"You should ask your cop friends to resign since they’re racist and evil," he said on X at the time.

Supporters of Palestine gather at Harvard University to show their support for Palestinians in Gaza at a rally in Cambridge, Massachusetts, on October 14, 2023. Thousands of Palestinians sought refuge on October 14 after Israel warned them to evacuate the northern Gaza Strip before an expected ground offensive against Hamas, one week on from the deadliest attack in Israeli history. (Joseph Prezioso/AFP via Getty Images)

As rioters and looters wreaked havoc in major metropolitan areas nationwide, Davis defended the chaos.

"Something to keep in mind: rioting and looting are parts of democracy just like voting and marching," he said on X. "The people WILL be heard."

In the same year, around the time President Donald Trump tested positive for COVID-19, Davis said on X that he didn't blame people who wished Trump ill. He followed that post with a second, captioned "But also, f--- that guy," attaching a meme that said "If he dies, he dies."

Peter D'Abrosca is a politics reporter at Fox News Digital.
